name: ChartQA
description: A large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts with visual and logical reasoning, covering 9,608 human-written questions and 23,111 machine-generated questions over 20,882 real-world charts curated from four online sources.
creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
citeAs: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque. ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning. arXiv:2203.10244v1, 2022.
rai:dataCollection: The benchmark was constructed by crawling charts from four online sources: Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD, to ensure diversity in topics and chart styles. For the Pew dataset, only chart images were crawled because underlying data tables were not available. For the other three sources, the authors extracted underlying data tables, metadata such as title and chart type, SVG files, and associated text descriptions. Bounding box information of chart elements was extracted from SVG files to train data extraction models.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of real-world chart images from Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD; for three of these sources the authors also extracted underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and text descriptions.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors extracted bounding boxes of chart elements from SVG files to train data extraction models. They also generated additional QA pairs from Statista human-written summaries using T5 models for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation. Invalid generated questions were filtered out using a heuristic that removed questions whose answers could not be found in the chart data table, and the machine-generated test set was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For Pew, only chart images were collected because data tables were unavailable. For the other sources, underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and text descriptions were extracted. Bounding boxes of chart elements were extracted from SVG files. For machine-generated QA pairs, generated questions were filtered using a heuristic based on whether the answer could be found in the chart data table, and the test set was manually cleaned to remove invalid questions.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Two annotation procedures were used: (1) human-authored QA collection using Amazon Mechanical Turk, and (2) machine generation of QA pairs from Statista human-written summaries. In the AMT task, workers were asked to write two questions per chart image focusing on compositional questions and visual questions, and provide answers. The same questions were then answered by another annotator. If both answers exactly matched, the answer was accepted; otherwise, the authors manually checked the answers and selected the final correct answer. In each HIT, workers also verified two previously asked questions by other workers and provided two new QA pairs. For machine-generated QA pairs, a pre-trained T5 model fine-tuned on SQuAD was used for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation from human-written chart summaries.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For human-authored QA pairs, agreement between crowd workers based on exact matches was 61.04%. Because exact match does not account for typos or lexical variations, the authors manually checked 500 random samples and found agreement to be 78.55% when considering typos and lexical variations. For machine-generated QA pairs, after heuristic filtering, manual analysis of 1,250 QA pairs found that 86.64% were complete, answerable, and correct given the chart. The machine-generated test set was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions.
rai:annotatorDemographics: AMT workers were selected with an acceptance rate of 95% and at least 5000 accomplished HITs, and were further filtered using a pretest. The paper also states compensation was based on the U.S. minimum wage and annotations were anonymized.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 model fine-tuned on SQuAD for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/vis-nlp/ChartQA
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes charts from sources covering topics such as social and economic issues, demographic trends, public opinion, politics, health, and society. The paper explicitly mentions demographic trends and public opinion as part of the chart sources.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors state that their models can be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications. They also note that they cannot guarantee model outputs will always be correct.
rai:dataBiases: Politics is a common topic among all sources, particularly in the Pew dataset where nearly half of charts are about U.S. Politics & Policy (45.4%). Bar charts are the most common chart type across the dataset. The authors also note that machine-generated questions may be invalid because of mismatch between training and test domains.
rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark contains challenging real-world charts and human-written questions, and model performance is lower than on previous datasets. The paper notes limitations including OCR and data extraction errors, especially for pie charts and diverse real-world styles; inability of current models to effectively handle nested operations; and input representations that do not fully capture chart structure. For machine-generated questions, some generated questions were incomplete or not answerable from the chart, requiring heuristic filtering and manual cleaning.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is presented as a benchmark for chart question answering and is split into training, validation, and test sets for both human-written (ChartQA-H) and machine-generated (ChartQA-M) subsets.
